📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you want the most portable way to listen to music on the go, then the best earbuds are a fantastic way to do it. They're tiny, often comfortable, and offer noise cancellation to keep the sounds of the outside world at bay.

It has been revealed that at the moment, the AirPods Pro 3 take the crown. But we've spent hundreds of hours testing earbuds to find out which are the best around if you want more than just Apple's offering. They come at a range of different price points to suit any budget, too.

Each entry on the list has a quick read section, giving you a brief overview of the buds, followed by longer reviews so that you can get a better idea of how they perform. So let's get straight into it. These are the best wireless earbuds you can buy right now.

We've spent 20 years testing the best earbuds (and the worst; you don't know until they're in your ears) to help you find your next set of portable audio companions.

The expertise comes from a few places, including our expert reviewers Erin Bashford and Nikita Achanta, who lead our audio testing. Then there's me, Tammy Rodgers, and I've been testing audio equipment for over half a decade, including a time as Tom's Guide's Audio Editor.

Before any earbuds make their way to this guide, here's how we put them through their paces to make sure we only recommend sets we truly believe in and would use ourselves.

In a recent development, when you're looking for latest earbuds, there's a whole range of terminology brands will use to talk about specs and performance. To make things a bit easier, these are the most common terms that come up, and what they mean for you.

In a recent development, most earbuds come with Active Noise Cancellation (ANC). It uses audio magic and some very clever algorithms to quiet the outside world and make your commute more manageable.

The earbuds have mics on the outside to pick up external noise. As this passes into your ear, the earbuds generate an opposing frequency to cancel the sound before you hear it. Sometimes this can change the sound of your music, so we'll report when the ANC is either too weak or too invasive.

Industry observers note that the EQ, or equalization, allows you to customize the way the earbuds sound. Usually, this means a series of sliders or dials in the companion smartphone app for adjusting the bass, mids or treble. Some manufacturers give you preset EQ options, which save you from getting lost in sliders or graphs.

Recent findings suggest that these are the different sounds that make up your music. You'll generally see them divided into three simple sections: the lows, the mids, and the highs. The lows are the bass frequencies. Think bass guitars and kick drums. You want them to be impactful and low.

The mids are the main parts of your music, like vocals, guitars, and synths. Because they're so important, you want them to be thick and wide. Finally, the highs are cymbals and other higher sounds. These should be crisp and clear.

Tammy is one of Tom's Guide's Buying Guide Editors. She also spends a great deal of her time testing the best earbuds, evaluating them for sound, ANC, comfort and battery life. She's always got at least three pairs of earbuds to choose from at her desk.

Erin is a proud music nerd and needs the best earbuds around. Whether it's eardrum-shedding nu-metal or tranquil folk, she'll listen to it. If a pair of earbuds has awesome sound quality, bouncy ANC and are comfortable? It's an immediate recommendation, regardless of price or brand.

As a music nerd, Nikita is always listening to music. As a reviews writer, she tests earbuds by pushing battery life to the limit and analyzing performance across various genres to answer the question: Are they good value for money? She listens to music almost throughout the day and plays guitar and bass, so she knows how to determine whether a pair of buds reproduces sound well.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The AirPods Pro 3 are the latest version of Apple's popular flagship earbuds. The stem-like design remains, but you get better battery life, an improved fit and more detailed sound. This makes them a worthy upgrade from the AirPods Pro 2, and the gold standard for wireless earbuds. Plus, the Pro 3 have a built-in heart rate monitor and Live Translation (if you have a compatible iPhone).

It has been revealed that the AirPods Pro 2 were excellent, but soon aged out compared to the competition. Now, the AirPods Pro 3 have arrived to conquer all and lay waste to Sony and Bose. And, despite a couple of minor flaws, they're right now the best wireless earbuds you can buy right now.

These are the very best earbuds that Apple has ever made. They've got some key updates over the previous model, for one. There's the extended battery life of eight hours, improved sound quality, and superior noise canceling to keep the noise of your commute at bay.

Those upgrades have materialized in a pair of buds that stun in sound and make sure that your office is a whole lot more tolerable when you're getting on with your day. They lose out to the Sony and Bose due to a lack of codec support for Android devices, but there really is nothing better if you're an iPhone user.

It has been revealed that the AirPods Pro 3 improve on the old model in the sound department. They've still got Apple's more neutral sound signature built in, but find more detail and extra bass depth than the older pair.

Sources indicate that they've got a very solid soundstage as well. They're on par with the Sony buds, and better than the Bose alternatives — although there are still options out there that sound better.

Spatial Audio for movies with an Apple TV is still a great way to watch your content, and just as easy to connect up. It works well for music as well, especially when you listen to your music on Apple Music.

According to recent reports, the buds have been shrunk this time around, and as a result, have a very comfortable fit. The silicone eartips have been infused with foam for a softer and more comfortable finish, and they mold better to the inner part of your ear.

In a recent development, that means you can wear them for extended periods of time. The sweat and water resistance means you won't have to worry about wearing them when you go to work out, either, hitting an IP57 rating this time around.

Industry observers note that the AirPods Pro have always had 'good enough' ANC; powerful but not exceptional. But that changed with the Pro 3, which now almost compete with the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2, but don't quite beat out Bose's buds.

In a recent development, still, it's very good and blocks out all the major noises of your commute or your busy office. It's on par with the Sony WF-1000XM6 — both are excellent noise-canceling options.

It has been revealed that transparency mode is very good as well, and boosts the battery life by another couple of hours. Nice.

There isn't an app for the AirPods Pro 3, but you can easily adjust their settings from the iPhone settings menu. There, you'll find all their features along with options to enhancement the firmware and change the sound.

Although you can pair the AirPods Pro 3 to an Android phone, I wouldn't really recommend it. You get the bare minimum on a non-Apple phone; a wireless connection. You can't adjust settings, so I'd only suggest the AirPods with an Android phone if you're in a bind.

It has been revealed that much like on the Apple Watch, the battery life for the AirPods has remained stuck for years, allowing the competition to lead ahead. The AirPods 3 Pro buck the trend and, for once, increase the per-bud battery life up to eight hours of ANC listening.

It has been revealed that that's a two-hour increase and puts them almost in line with the Sony and Bose sets. If you switch over to the transparency mode, you get 10 hours of battery life, more than pretty much anything else at their price point. That also means you can use the latest Live Translation feature for longer.

It has been revealed that the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds boast excellent sound quality, customizable EQ, and great battery life. Noise cancellation excels, and the design is also great. These are a highly recommended upgrade for superior quiet and sound control.

Industry observers note that when following up on a highly successful pair of earbuds, there are a couple of things you do. First, you make things better — more features, better sound quality. Then you improve the design — make the fit better, improve the looks.

That’s the WF-1000XM6, Sony’s follow-up to the WF-1000XM5. The AirPods of this generation make a better case for your money if you wield an iPhone, but the XM6 are great for just about everyone else. Just like their predecessor, they’re a fantastic all-rounder, with great specs, sound and ANC.

In a recent development, our four-star review highlights that they’re not entirely perfect. The new case design is a bit odd and makes fitting them into a pocket a chore, and they’re more expensive than the previous model, but those are our only major criticisms.

The sound quality is, as you might expect for something from the WF-1000X series, very good, with support for LDAC. Sony’s excellent DSEE Extreme audio upscaler is here as well, and works a treat. The ANC boasts a massive improvement, too, although Bose still has Sony beat for out-and-out noise performance.

They’re a wonderful pair of comfortable buds with plenty of battery life — there’s little more you could ask for, apart from a discount.

In a recent development, they may seem on the expensive side, but the upgrades in sound performance make them totally worth it. Sony is known for a warmer sound profile on their headphones, and these are a total joy to listen to.

They are only made better by using the personalized EQ settings on the earbuds, and there’s seriously no genre that these buds can’t cope with.

Your favorite songs will sound a lot more detailed, and it’s really awesome to get a studio sound from earbuds instead of having to rely on studio headphones to do the job.

In a recent development, these earbuds are superbly comfortable, and you get a bunch of different eartip options in the box to get the best seal and best security. You can do a fit test to make sure everything fits.

I can wear these buds for hours at a time — they’re seriously comfortable, and they’re lightweight so they never weigh me down.

ANC differs depending on personal experience with these buds. My own experience was amazing, and I couldn’t fault them at all. They made a long travel day on a plane, train, and bus completely silent.

However, another one of my colleagues who tried them out was still able to hear the sounds of traffic moving around. I think it’s all about the eartip fit, so this is an extremely crucial process to complete.

If you buy this set, just make sure you use the Optimal Earbud Tips feature in the Sound Connect App to get the best fit, and ensure your ANC is working properly.

Sources indicate that the Sound Connect app is one of the most user-friendly I’ve tried. Once you get the hang of things and organize the app to suit the settings you need to use the most, it’s incredibly handy and makes using the earbuds so much better.

The app is where you do all the earbud fit tests and personalized EQ tests to make the overall experience with the buds so much better.

According to recent reports, you get eight hours of battery per bud with ANC and 24 hours with the charging case. This is pretty standard and matches up with Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 and the Sony WF-1000XM5.

Industry observers note that the A100 SE are all about sound — pure and simple. There's no feature bloat, no extra AI things, just a pair of great-sounding earbuds with epic battery life. The ANC has fallen behind the competition a little this time around, but they're a great pick for a fantastic price.

Sources indicate that the first Cambridge A100 are some of my favorite wireless earbuds — and the SE version are no different. They come in at a price that doesn’t break the bank and offer some of the best sound quality around. For sub-$150, they sound better than buds that cost twice as much — there’s a reason we constantly compare them to the AirPods Pro 3 and others in the review.

They’re refined and classy in their sound, as befits a legacy British Hi-Fi brand. The soundstage is expansive and well layered, and vocals shine. Erin loved the dynamism and vibrancy in her review, noting the accuracy and faithfulness of their representation. High praise indeed.

It has been revealed that we had no problems with the comfort as well, and wore them extensively during the testing period. The case is compact and well-shaped (perfect for fitting them into a tighter pocket), and the app is useful and well laid out, though simplistic.

In a recent development, there are just a couple of problems. The ANC isn’t quite up there with other options at a similar price, and the Dolby Atmos mode is, like, bad. But beyond those two bugbears, the A100 SE are the perfect successor to some of our favorite earbuds and a top-notch value pick.

Recent findings suggest that cambridge has fired a warning shot at just about every other audio manufacturer with the A100 SE. The first model sounded good, but these sound even better. We love how dynamic and clear the buds sound, and the seven-band custom EQ means you can really dial them in.

They sound better even than more expensive earbuds, and take the fight to options that cost $100-$150 more. That’s the focus of the buds: excellent sound, forget the frills.

Recent findings suggest that there’s warmth here, but it doesn’t overshadow the rest of the sound. Everything is still very clear and expansive, with solid instrument separation. We’re big fans of the sound.

We scored the buds well for comfort, thanks to their smooth shape and range of different eartips. For the most part, we were able to wear them for long periods without them getting uncomfortable. We didn’t want to rip them out after the workday.

But those with small ears might struggle a little more. These aren’t small buds, and for one tester, they pressed on some parts of their ear. They weren’t uncomfortable, but they knew they were there.

In a recent development, the ANC isn’t going to win them any awards. It’s fine and blocks out some noise, but it’s not as all-encompassing as other options available. If you’re looking for something that blocks out everything, then you might want to think about Sony’s similarly priced options.

Still, if ANC isn’t a priority but you still want some noise blocking, then you won’t find anything to complain about — and the noise-canceling compromise is worth making for that excellent sound.

Cambridge’s app is fine, but we did have some problems with some of the features. It became a little buggy at times, with some features not working as they should. A quick restart fixed the issue, but it’s still worth mentioning.

What we really liked, however, was the complete omission of extra feature bloat. There’s everything you might need — an EQ, ANC controls, and that surround mode — but there’s nothing extra. No AI feature, no voice control thing, just what you actually need when using the buds. That’s refreshing.

Battery life is a particular strength of Cambridge's headphones and earbuds. Here, we’ve got 39 hours on tap, 10 hours of bud life. That’s more than just about anything else out there, including buds that cost a whole lot more. It even takes some over-ear headphones to task, and they generally have buds beat for staying power.

Everything charges up rapidly, and we found that the battery figures matched up to expectations when we did all of our testing. If you want something that lasts a long time, the A100 SE are a great option.

The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the fitness lover's dream. A very comfortable, secure fit so that they stay in place no matter how you move around, and great sound quality to power your workouts. The built-in heart rate monitor is a great cherry on top.

In a recent development, now, I'll be the first to admit that I'm not a fitness expert — but I sure am an earbuds expert. As earbuds, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are great; there's a reason we ranked them as the best workout headphones you can get right now. They've got excellent ANC from the AirPods Pro 2, and there's some great sound for a solid audio experience.

Given that I'm not a fitness expert, I also spoke to someone who is, so that we can get a picture of why they're on the list. From my review, our fitness expert Nick stated:"I genuinely believe that the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are outstanding sports headphones and would be top of my list for people who need an earhook to keep their buds in place during runs and other workouts.".

Recent findings suggest that it's thanks to those secure-fit hooks that keep the earbuds in place no matter how much you run or move around. The heart rate monitor is a nice extra, but we were slightly disappointed with its accuracy.

For all kinds of exercise, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are an excellent earbud option for everyone.

In a recent development, while not high-fidelity, there's a rhythmic energy to the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 that's infectious. They've got some great bass presence, as you might expect, but they're also good in the upper register too.

Recent findings suggest that they fall down slightly in the mid-range, with a dip in the upper mid-range. That can take the edge off guitars and other instruments, although R&B listeners aren't going to notice too much.

There's head-tracked Apple Spatial Audio as well for Apple Music listeners, and it works well. It does a number on your battery though, so bear that in mind.

Thanks to their excellent earhook, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 aren't going anywhere when you do your exercise. It can be a challenge to get them in place, but they're very stable once in.

It has been revealed that the buds themselves are comfortable for long periods of wear as well, thanks to the silicone eartip options that you get in the box. The fit finder in the app is good as well, so that you can dial them in perfectly.

The ANC on board is very similar to that which you'll find in the AirPods Pro 2. That means that they're not quite up to speed with the likes of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 or the Sony WF-1000XM6, but they still manage to block plenty of noise.

It has been revealed that the transparency modes work well enough, although I found that voices occasionally became fuzzy or tricky to hear depending on the surrounding noise. A shame, but not a deal breaker.

Sources indicate that on Apple devices, the Beats are integrated into your settings menu. It works well, with all the options at your fingertips. Android consumers have to use the Beats app, which is fine, although we did find some heart rate monitor weirdness on Android devices.

It has been revealed that both methods let you control the ANC and dial in the EQ settings. They're simple, but they work well enough. Android people might find the occasional crash, however.

The battery life of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 is exemplary. They feature 10 hours of battery life in the buds themselves, beating out many other options on this list.

That's perfect for long-distance runners and cyclists, or gym-goers who want something that will take them to the gym, last through their exercise, and then take them home again. We found those battery life claims were true in our review. Pop them in the charging case for 45 hours of staying power.

Improving on almost every metric compared to the original model (except battery), the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 are an in-ear noise-canceling triumph. Boosts to ANC and sound quality make them an even better buy than the first model, and the price hasn't increased to match the improved performance.

Recent findings suggest that the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds were my favorite release of 2024, and the Gen 2 are now my favorite of 2026. They've improved on pretty much everything over the first model, with the only exception being the unchanged battery life — but it's that world-silencing ANC that really takes them over the edge.

They remain the very best way to listen to music without disruption when you're traveling. That busy train carriage? Silenced. The office? Quietened completely. With that signature orchestral swell, you're in your own world, free to listen to your tunes.

Sound is much better this time around, although you'll still want to adjust the EQ in the Bose app. And you'll be listening comfortably for their entire 6-hour battery life thanks to their incredibly comfortable fit.

I gave them 4.5 stars when I reviewed them, thanks to that all-conquering ANC and solid sound quality. They lose out in the battery department to the XM6, opting instead for out-and-out ANC performance — and there's nothing better to block noise.

The bassy sound of prior Bose earbuds is still here, but it's been refined slightly this time around. There's more detail retrieval, and the soundstage has been extended, but the bass weighting is still very much present.

It has been revealed that I've found that dipping into the Bose apps' EQ is a must with any of the brand's headphones. From there, I adjust the bass down slightly and the highs up a few notches to increase the detail and reduce any muddiness. They sound great out of the box, but these improvements make them sound even better.

There's also Immersive Audio, Bose's spatial audio setting. Some like its ability to make music sound much larger, but I find it thins out vital frequencies. It also tanks the battery by two hours, making them last an even shorter time.

It has been revealed that yeah, they're still some of the most comfortable buds you can buy. I've been able to wear them for hours and hours at a time without the need to adjust the fit or take them out for a break — they're a lovely thing to have in your ears.

According to recent reports, it's all down to the fitting options. There are loads of different silicone tips, and the fit is further improved by the rubber fins you can attach to the edge. They're secure as well, so they won't fall out should you get headbanging or dancing.

Recent findings suggest that the ANC is the best around — there's nothing that comes close. That's high praise given how good the previous model was at keeping out unwanted sounds, but Bose has somehow made it even better. It's a bit like magic.

In a recent development, you can choose different levels for the noise canceling, but I prefer to leave it on the top level. That way, I don't have to worry about any noise making its way through at all, and I can enjoy my music to the max.

Sources indicate that bose's app is one of the better options around. It's very well laid out, and everything is clearly labeled so that you don't get confused. It even reveals you what's playing, although I'm not entirely sure how useful that feature is.

It's where you'll find all of the EQ options, noise control, and different sound modes. I particularly like how the app knows what color your buds are — and even lets you name them.

Battery life remains a weak point in the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2's armor. We've still only got six hours' worth of life here, which pales in comparison to some of the competition.

The WF-1000XM6 last for eight hours, a whole two hours more than the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. You can't even turn the ANC off to boost the battery life — six hours is all you're going to get.

The Noble Fokus Amadeus are all about one thing and one thing only — their sound quality. Sound quality that blows just about everything else you can buy out of the water. Their ANC is very good, and they're very comfortable, but you buy these for their sound quality.

Recent findings suggest that the Noble Fokus Amadeus are not cheap. They're more than the AirPods Pro 3, and $50 more than the XM6 and the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds. They're not the most expensive earbuds around, but you should be ready to shell out if you want a pair.

And you will want a pair, because they've dethroned other excellent-sounding earbuds with their incredibly well-rounded sound signature that dishes out masterful amounts of detail while providing plenty of low-end punch.

Sources indicate that for the price, this is about as close to wired earbuds as you're going to get. The crisp detail is utterly sublime, their mids are fat and juicy, and the bass is tight, controlled, and impactful. An audiophile's wireless dream, one might say, and the fresh earbud sound quality standard that all else must be measured against.

Sources indicate that the price means they're out of reach for many users, but as I discovered in my testing, they're well worth their higher price thanks to a very good all-round package. The battery is good, and the ANC matches up — there's very little to get sad about here.

In a recent development, the absolute best thing about the Noble Fokus Amadeus is their sound profile. Thanks to the Audiodo profile in the app it means they sound amazing for everyone too, catering the sound for specific hearing needs.

There are details in my tracks I'd not heard for a while thanks to the impressive detail, and the mids bring plenty of body to listening. The bass kicks and barks with impressive control, notably adding more for drum and bass in particular.

According to recent reports, the sound is effortlessly spaced apart for a wide soundstage, and the instruments are very well separated. They sound better than absolutely everything on this list — they're hard to get hold of, but it's worth every single effort when you do.

It has been revealed that the Amadeus come with a range of different fitting options in the box for a very comfortable fit. They're more shaped and molded than other options as well, making them easier to wear for longer periods of time.

My favorite fitting options are the flanged tips because they not only improve the sound and the ANC, but they stay in place better than the other options.

According to recent reports, while not quite as good as the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2, the ANC is still very good, especially if you opt to use the included flanged tips. It blocks out plenty of noise, focusing on low-end sounds like bus engines.

Transparency mode is nice and natural as well, and makes it easier to talk to shop clerks and bus drivers without needing to take buds out of your ears. There's perhaps a little more noise than some might like, but it's otherwise very good.

The Noble Fokus app is very simple and lacks some of the more in-depth modes and settings of some of the competition. It's very easy to use, though, and offers everything you actually need.

Industry observers note that there's the Audiodo sound customization, as well as a very in-depth EQ to really dial the sound in to your preferred listening curve. You can also change the noise-canceling mode and adjust the volume. Beyond that, there's not much else. At least there's a nice picture of your buds.

Battery life is very solid in the Fokus Amadeus. The buds last for eight hours with the ANC turned on, and 12 hours if you turn the ANC off. They charge swiftly in the case, which provides a total of 42 hours of charge. That's amongst the very best battery life on the list.

Wireless charging is the cherry on top, and a 10-minute quick charge for two hours of use is a nice bonus too.

Recent findings suggest that CMF's latest pair of budget buds are sub-$50 heroes. They pack in loads of premium features, like great customization and even a form of spatial audio. They sound great, fit well, and come in a range of different colors. What's not to like?

This is a spot that’s likely to be occupied by CMF for some time — the brand's budget buds are just that much better than everyone else's. For just $50 (and often less thanks to significant price drops during deal events), you get earbuds that feel like they’re worth a whole lot more.

According to recent reports, CMF has packed in a whole range of great features. There’s sound customization from Dirac, which generally deals with premium Hi-Fi equipment. You get a form of spatial audio to make your music sound bigger, and there’s even great ANC to keep the outside world at bay.

According to recent reports, the sound is the most impressive thing here, though. They sound like a pair of buds that cost loads more, and once you’ve gone through the Dirac sound tuning, there’s very little better for under $100. Premium buds — low price.

Industry observers note that thanks to CMF’s use of Dirac, the CMF Buds 2 sound excellent. While the core sound is very good, with plenty of bass for impact and revealing detail for interest, the EQ settings kick things up a notch. We’ve described it as “breathing newly introduced life into your songs” — and you’d be hard-pressed to find something at this price that sounds better.

Industry observers note that they’re great for a wide range of genres as a result. We spun up everything from the heaviest of metal to breezy folk and classical, and the buds didn’t skip a beat. They’re as meaty as they are delicate — extremely impressive considering the price.

Industry observers note that there’s nothing else that sounds like this at the low price point at which they sit. Even without Dirac, they’re impressive — although you’ll want to run the tuning engine to get the most out of them possible.

According to recent reports, thanks to a multitude of fitting options in the box and a great bud design, the CMF Buds 2 are very comfortable. There are three different sizes, and we found that the ‘small’ size option was perfect for even very small ears.

According to recent reports, there are comfier buds out there, but we had little problem wearing them all day during our testing. More expensive buds might feel slightly nicer in the ear, but these still feel great for the price.

You can’t expect Bose-level ANC for $50, but you’ll be immediately impressed by the noise-canceling packed into the CMF Buds 2. It does a very good job of keeping the outside world at bay, with some very impressive noise blocking.

In a recent development, the transparency mode is good too, making it easy to hear what's going on without a robotic edge. They cut down slightly with the ANC during calls — while your voice will be clear, your call partner will be able to hear everything going on around you.

The Nothing X app is excellent. It's super simple to navigate, with easy access to all the features in the buds. There’s a home screen, and then various menus that are clearly labelled. It’s a must-install if you pick up the CMF Buds 2.

This is where you find the Dirac tuning menu, as well as other settings. Those include the ANC settings, fit test, spatial audio, and touch control settings.

11 hours of use in the buds is very solid indeed, and our testing showed no reason to dispute CMF's claims. The case contains 55 hours of use, so you can charge the buds about four times from empty. This is good battery life for buds, better than even some of the more premium options.

Samsung's latest buds bring a less AirPods-like case design and excellent sound quality to the table. Some settings and options are locked off for everyone but Galaxy device users, but they're a great option for the Samsung faithful.

Not one to miss out on a good earbud battle, Samsung’s Galaxy Buds 4 Pro bring a whole host of features to the Samsung crowd who want something that seamlessly integrates with their phone.

They sound great, and Samsung’s audio upscaling tech is almost as good as Sony’s for improving weaker streams from the likes of Spotify and YouTube Music. That looks like the place Samsung has put the most work into the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro, improving massively over the older model.

Not quite as much work seems to have gone into the battery life, unfortunately. There are only around seven hours on tap with ANC turned on, which lags behind the key competition like the eight hours of the AirPods Pro 3. Still, you get more charge in the case at 30 hours.

Samsung has also packed in some very solid ANC, with loads of clever modes if you wield a Galaxy handset. That’s where their true value lies. There are a bunch of features that only Samsung consumers will appreciate, like AI translation that only works with Galaxy phones.

Industry observers note that if you’re a Galaxy phone user, then the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro were likely already on your shortlist. Thanks to our testing, we can tell you that they’re a great pair of buds that’ll pair with your device perfectly.

“Overall, the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro sound utterly divine” is how Erin finished off the sound portion of the buds review. That’s thanks to rich bass, excellent mids, and great vocals, giving you a top-notch audio experience.

Industry observers note that detail heads might prefer the slightly tighter AirPods or Sony WF-1000XM6, but these sound better than the likes of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. Their AI sound enhancement works great with lower-quality streams as well.

Thanks to some solid shaping, the Buds 4 Pro are comfortable to wear for long periods of time. There are plenty of fitting options in the box as well to make sure that you’ll find the best fit for you, no matter what shape your ear canals are.

Some with smaller ears might find their slightly larger bodies tighter, but it’s not enough to make them in any way uncomfortable.

The noise canceling is excellent, blocking out all the noise that we could throw at them. They perform about the same as the AirPods and Sony competition, making for more relaxing journeys while wearing them.

Transparency mode is also good, and doesn’t make any of the incoming noise sound robotic. The ANC performance might not be quite as impressive as the Bose buds, but it’s more than a match for the Sony and Apple alternatives.

Some of the headline features, like the AI settings and call enhancement, are only available for Galaxy S23 models and newer. The buds use the Samsung settings menu itself rather than a dedicated app on these devices, and it works well.

Recent findings suggest that there is a Samsung app for other devices, and it's fine. You can control the ANC and other settings, and upgrade the firmware. Still, there are better app experiences for non-Galaxy users, like the Sony and Bose apps.

Battery life is fine. It’s not as good as the eight hours you get from the AirPods or the Sony WF buds, but the seven hours on tap is more than enough to get you through the day. The 30 hours in the charging case, though, make up for the slightly lacking battery life of the buds.

Industry observers note that not every pair of earbuds we test can land on the best list — otherwise, this would just be a list of earbuds that are available to buy. But some are still pretty good and worth considering if you need more options.

Thanks to some key upgrades (mostly in the sound department), the AirPods 5 are a great pair of earbuds, especially with the newly introduced lower price compared to the AirPods 4. The battery life just isn't good enough, however, and compatibility with Android remains an issue that holds them back from a full-chested recommendation.

The EarFun Air Pro 4 bring some excellent features at a bargain price. For a lot less than $100, you get solid ANC, great sound, and a very comfortable fit. They last for ages thanks to their 7.5-hour per-bud battery life, and support loads of hi-res codecs so that your music always sounds its very best.

Read our full EarFun Air Pro 4 review.

Sources indicate that the Cambridge Audio Melomania M100 are wonderful earbuds with impeccable sound and a monstrous 52-hour battery life. But the ANC isn't as effective as we'd like, and the case is large and cumbersome to carry around.

Read our full Cambridge Audio Melomania M100 review.

Sources indicate that sony's WF-C710N are well-priced buds that bring some great specs to the table and don't cost the earth. Their ANC is solid, and the sound is very good. We found them comfortable to wear for long periods of time. Whether you like the transparent blue design will probably help you decide if these are right for you.

Read our full Sony WF-C710N review.

The Liberty 5 Pro Max are Soundcore's first entry into the premium earbud space. It is largely successful, with good sound and solid ANC. But at this price, the AirPods Pro 3 or Sony WF-1000XM6 are better value for immersive audio with ANC.

Read our full Soundcore Anker Liberty 5 Pro Max review.

In a recent development, before we make a recommendation about any pair of wireless earbuds, we want to make sure that we've put them through their paces. It helps us find out how good they'll be when you find them in your hands, and makes sure that we can pen our informative, buying advice-packed reviews.

In a recent development, it's all work — no fun. Listening to our favorite music for hours on end to test the sound, taking the earbuds out and about on day trips to test their long-term comfort and ANC algorithm. In all seriousness, we put a lot of effort into making sure that you'll be happy with a purchase you make after reading our buying guides and reviews.

Here are the key factors in our testing and how we evaluate each pair of earbuds that falls across our desks.

It has been revealed that earbuds are going to be jammed directly into your ear holes, so one of the most vital things that we test is how comfortable they are over long periods of time, and how difficult it is to dial in the fit. How many bud bits do you get in the box, and are they easy to fit on the buds? Are they loose? Are there extra fitting options like earhooks?

Recent findings suggest that to find out, we put the buds through their paces. We try out a range of the tips that come with the budsto find the perfect fit that makes the ANC excellent and sound good. After all, if they don't seal well inside of your ear, you're not going to get the best out of your buds. We report our findings, like how easy it was to get the perfect fit, and how comfy they are when dialed in.

Sources indicate that then we test their long-term comfort. That means wearing them for hours during a work day, so that we can see how they feel when they're worn for hours on end. If they start impacting certain pressure points in the ear, we'll notice, and it'll go into our review. We're looking for earbuds that can't be felt during wear, so that you forget you're wearing them.

According to recent reports, this is my favorite thing to test. Hours and hours of my favorite tunes played into my ears while I work, and I don't have to make excuses to my boss about why I need to be doing it. Excellent news. When we test the audio quality of a pair of buds, we play the Tom's Guide testing playlist on Qobuz so that we can get a good picture of how they sound with some top-quality hi-res tracks to put them through their paces.

We listen at first in a quieter environment so that we can get an idea of how they sound in a vacuum without the ANC to cause potential problems. We compare the earbuds to the sound profiles of those in the best list above, and then we write down our findings for the full review.

Then, we take the earbuds out with the ANC to see if it changes the sound. It might all sound like we're having fun, but there is a point to it all. It gives us a clear picture of the buds' performance in an everyday use case, so that we can see how they'll serve you if you decide you'd like to buy a pair.

Pretty much every pair of earbuds that you can buy today comes with some form of ANC (unless you buy some of the very cheapest ones at the very end of a lengthy Amazon search, you madman), and we want to make sure that it performs well in a variety of use cases.

Recent findings suggest that how do we do it? By taking the earbuds with us wherever we go. That could mean on all our daily commutes, to see if they perform well on the train, or out for hikes so we can see how well they handle normal atmospheric noise. Maybe we're going on a flight — then we can test how well they handle loud engines and crying children.

Once we've thoroughly tested how much noise they block, we also test the transparency modes when we go to buy our tickets or a bag of candies from the grocery store. We look out for how clear the voice of our conversation partner is, and whether they're audible through any other noise. We're also looking out for the quality of the audio that's being pumped in. Is it too loud? Again, we note down our findings for the review.

Industry observers note that finally, we want to make sure that the ANC doesn't change the sound of the music too much. After all, you want your music to sound great, and if the ANC changes things too much, it can create annoying sonic issues.

Given that your earbuds are often going to pull double duty as a form of hands-free calling system, we want to ensure that they're going to be good at it. We make a whole bunch of calls to check things out.

We're looking out for a couple of different things. First of all, we want to make sure that we can hear our call partner well, and that they're coming through clearly. We listen out for clarity and judge whether we can hear them properly throughout the duration of the call, and whether their voice sounds natural.

Industry observers note that then we ask our call partners how we sound. Can they hear us properly, or do the noises of our environment make it hard to hear what we're saying? We note down our findings, and then we report back on them in our review to give you an idea of how they'll perform if you want to take (or make) a call.

We know that manufacturers sometimes have a habit of overestimating their battery life figures. To make sure that you're getting the best information possible, we spend the time testing the battery life claims and whether they ring true. We listen to the buds for hours on end, and count how many hours we used them before they needed to go back into their case. We do this with ANC turned on and with the volume at a comfortable level.

For charging cases and very long-lasting buds, we extrapolate battery data in a different way. We measure how long we've used them, and then compare that with how much life we've got left. This gives us a good picture of how the battery is going to last in the long run, and whether you'll get those rated claims.

In a recent development, hopefully, we've managed to curate a list of wireless earbuds that hit the mark for you. But if you're still not sure how to choose between them, these are some additional pointers.

What do you want out of your buds?

Industry observers note that there are as many reasons to buy earbuds as there are earbuds themselves. You need to work out what you're looking for first and foremost — it's why I've divided the list up into the most crucial headline features.

It has been revealed that do you want the best sound, and would you be willing to give up some battery life and pay a bit more for it? If not, then you should go for the best earbuds overall, but if you don't mind some compromise, then you should go for the best-sounding earbuds.

It's notable to make a list of the features that are most important to you, and then work out from there which of the earbuds on the list fit those criteria the best. After all, what might be the best for one person might not be the best for you.

Do you want headphones or earbuds?

If you're looking for the most compact, easily transported audio device around, then the best earbuds are probably going to be right for you. But there are a couple of things to remember: they're going to live inside your ears, and not everyone likes the feeling of in-ears after longer periods of listening.

Industry observers note that if you'd prefer something more comfortable for longer periods of wear that offers more battery life, and potentially better audio quality, you should consider some of the best wireless headphones. They might cost a bit more, but you might be more comfortable.

Recent findings suggest that repairability is becoming ever more notable, as we try to find new ways to lengthen the life of our devices, but also look after the planet that we call home. Repairing products is great for both, and it's important to consider it when buying new tech.

Unfortunately, earbuds are one of those products that are extremely rarely user-repairable. Thanks to their size and the amount of tech that companies have to pack into their buds, it's generally impossible to make the insides accessible to you or me.

Not all is lost, however — some manufacturers do offer some form of repair service, so you don't have to worry if your buds stop working. But this is still pretty rare, so if this is a priority for you, it's worth picking up a pair of the Fairphone Fairbuds 2.

In a recent development, there are seven user-repairable components; they cost less than $100 and come in two colors. Tom's Guide Managing Editor James Frew rated the first generation, but they weren't available in the U.S. That all changed with the Fairbuds 2, which you can buy directly from Fairphone.

According to recent reports, I talk about this on our best headphones list, but I think it's worth reiterating here. It's easy to get hooked on frequency response graphs and numbers, and think you're getting a surefire cheat code to finding the best-sounding earbuds.

You'll spot them as a pair of numbers in spec lists, like "15 Hz-22 kHz." The first number is how low the earbuds can go, and the second is how high they can go.

You might think that finding a pair with the greatest frequency range is going to net you a pair of excellent-sounding earbuds. While that can be true, it's not worth seeking out. Just because a pair of earbuds can go really low doesn't mean they're good at replicating those frequencies, and neither does it tell you about what's going on in the music itself.

According to recent reports, there's only one way to really tell how good a pair of earbuds is — and that's to give them a listen. Or, of course, you could read one of our excellent and informative earbuds reviews.

Candace Cameron Bure is getting real about why she signed on to cohost The View, despite her admitted lack of political knowledge.

“I was kind of duped. Raven will say the same thing,” Cameron Bure, 50, claimed during the Tuesday, November 24, episode of the “McBride Rewind” podcast, referring to former cohost Raven-Symoné.

The Full House alum alleged, “We were both told that the show was going to be pop culture and evergreen topics and not politics.”.

Recent findings suggest that while Cameron Bure said she had seen the talk show “in the past,” when she was approached to cohost The View it had just gotten a fresh producer and the team allegedly told her they were shifting the focus. (Cameron Bure was on the hosting panel for two seasons from 2015 to 2016.).

In a recent development, “I’d guest cohosted a couple of times. I didn’t realize I was actually auditioning for the seat,” Cameron Bure recalled of the process. “I came in a bit naive.”.

After guest cohosting the ABC series, Cameron Bure said she seemingly nailed the audition but she wasn’t sure she could handle being a full-time member of the panel.

“I was like, ‘I’m not comfortable talking about politics — I actually don’t even know if I know enough, but to actually verbalize all of the opinions,’” she recalled. “They go, ‘Actually we’re steering away from politics. We’re going a new direction in the show and it’s going to be much more about social complications, pop culture.’”.

Cameron Bure remembered the producers saying, “We might talk about politics here and there, but that’s not the focus of the show,” which is why she signed on.

The Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test season 5 winner claimed that what was presented to her before she joined soon shifted when she was in front of the camera.

“And then, it was like, it just turned into politics, and Donald Trump entered the [presidential] race, and, you know, all hell broke loose,” Cameron Bure said.

Outside of politics, Cameron Bure recalled talking with the powers at be about stepping into the shoes of Elisabeth Hasselbeck as the token conservative on the show.

“I knew I was going to be the conservative on the panel no matter what. Even with social topics, you can be morally conservative or not, but I know me,” Cameron Bure shared. “I’m me all the time. I’ve never changed who I am over the years. I’ve been very consistent my whole life and in my Christian faith and my beliefs.”.

It has been revealed that cameron Bure ultimately exited The View in 2016 after two seasons. Earlier this month, she returned as a guest after her Special Forces win and appeared to fit right back in with the women.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coros has unveiled the Vertix 4, an “expedition-focused” enhancement to the Vertix 2 and 2S. Coros claims it pairs the brand's brightest display yet with long battery life, and after unboxing it myself, I can definitely say it has a more refined feel that could indeed suit the office as well as the summit.

According to recent reports, this watch is being marketed as a major step up from the Vertix 2S, with an AMOLED display, a more refined design, satellite maps and, for the first time on a Coros watch, a built-in flashlight. The Vertix 4 will be available to buy starting on Black Friday, Nov. 27, but it won't exactly be at a discount: It costs $799, a $100 increase over the Vertix 2S.

According to recent reports, that price does still undercut the latest Garmin Fenix 9 line-up, which starts at $999, though some rivals are cheaper still. For instance, the Suunto Vertical 2 steel model costs $599, and the Garmin Fenix 8 is presently on sale for $749.99 at Amazon.

I've only just started testing the Vertix 4 and haven't even had enough time to get through its substantial battery life, but I can share some first impressions, particularly in how it compares with the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro that released earlier this year.

It has been revealed that built-in flashlights have become a must-have feature on premium sports watches, and now the Vertix 4 is the first Coros watch to get one. Coros has departed from the usual layout, though. Garmin, Suunto and Amazfit put the light on top of the watch, but Coros places it on the side, between the digital dial and the back button.

In a recent development, previous Vertix watches used a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display. MIP has advantages, most notably longer battery life, but I know I much prefer the vibrant display on AMOLED screens, like on the Vertix 4. It is the biggest visual change and a large part of why the watch looks more premium than its predecessors.

Coros claims up to 30 days in watch mode, or 10 days with the screen always on. It also quotes 48 hours of multi-band GPS tracking with the screen always on. I haven't had time to test these claims properly, so stay tuned.

Coros watches are high-quality sports watches, but don't expect to find all the little lifestyle features you've come to expect on a more traditional smartwatch:.

Music: It can store tracks, but only files you drag and drop onto the watch. It doesn't pair with streaming services.

Payments: There is no NFC payment support.

Watch faces: Customization is more limited than on rivals.

On paper, the Vertix 4 looks like a significant upgrade: a better display, a more attractive design, a flashlight and satellite maps, at a price well below the Fenix 9 line-up. The $100 increase and cheaper alternatives like the Suunto Vertical 2 and discounted Fenix 8 will matter to some buyers, as will the limited smart features.

It was a bug that's been caught and exterminated in patch 5.02. "Fixed an matter where werewolves could regenerate health too promptly on higher difficulty settings," the patch notes say, "making them impossible to defeat.".

Another problem some players had with The Witcher 3 Remastered was its lighting, with interiors in particular looking too dark while some other locations were washed-out flashbangs. Good news: "Fixed various lighting complications across multiple locations and cutscenes," the patch notes say, "including overly bright or dark areas, inconsistent lighting transitions and flickering." They've also "Fixed various lighting issues with hair when Path Tracing is enabled" and "Made various Path Tracing and Ray Reconstruction optimizations and visual improvements, including lighting, shadows, and water rendering.".

According to recent reports, that's all positive stuff, but the balance changes to various signs and mutations will be more controversial. The Remastered version introduced with buffs to Witcher signs that made them useful even if you didn't specialize in them, but it may have overdone things a little. This patch walks back some of the potential for you to dominate the entire game with an Aard build, though changes like reducing the Catalyst skill's bonus to Aard and Igni intensity by 10% don't seem like they'll totally change the way you play.

I get that people don't like skill nerfs in singleplayer games, but I can also see CD Projekt anticipating next year's Songs of the Past DLC. They don't want to hear a bunch of players say, "It sucked because I trivialized the whole thing with a broken build I got by copying a YouTuber." If some skill nerfs and a reduction to stamina regeneration in combat mean you have to drink more potions to get your signs off, it probably won't ruin your fun.

Sources indicate that oh, and if you couldn't complete your Gwent collection because Zoltan Chivay's card didn't show up, the patch notes say it'll now appear in the correct place under the Hanged Man's Tree in Velen. Time to go back and get that 100% achievement at last.

Another Gaming Console Price Hike Could Be Coming, Thanks To Upcoming Tariffs

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamespot

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US government has confirmed a upcoming round of tariffs targeting several major countries, including China, Japan, Vietnam, and European Union trading partners.
  • The US government has revealed a upcoming round of tariffs targeting several major countries, including China, Japan, Vietnam, and European Union trading partners.
  • According to recent reports, what does this mean for gaming hardware?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US government has confirmed a upcoming round of tariffs targeting several major countries, including China, Japan, Vietnam, and European Union trading partners. Under the proposed tariffs, import taxes will rise significantly, with China facing up to 40% when the new duties take effect next year. According to the BBC, some of the rates will be reduced because of tariff caps that US President Donald Trump has already agreed to, and individual countries could also face different levies. What does this mean for gaming hardware? Trump's first round of "Liberation Day" tariffs contributed to rising console prices, but the Supreme Court eventually struck them down. Big companies like Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo benefited from tariff refunds after the ruling, but they didn't pass the savings on to consumers. In Sony's case, it was estimated to get back $508 million in refunds from the US government. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4FatSqS3VYY&t=19s The new tariffs bypass the Supreme Court's ruling by using a different law, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the government to impose tariffs on countries that use unfair business practices. The law does require an investigation into specific trade practices before rates are set. If higher import taxes take effect, console companies could face much higher costs, and protecting their profits will likely mean consumers have to cover the difference. Nintendo, Sony, and Microsoft have moved much of their final assembly out of China and into Southeast Asia, especially Vietnam, to avoid earlier tariffs. However, key parts like batteries and power supplies still mostly come from China, and if tariffs on these parts rise, total production costs for consoles made outside China will go up even more. Some electronic goods could be exempt from tariffs, and manufacturers often stockpile inventory ahead of tariff deadlines to delay price changes. But with rising costs from the ongoing components shortage amid the AI boom and other global factors, console prices remain at risk. After the June announcement of steep console price hikes, Microsoft warned that Xbox console costs could rise again in 2027, and next-gen hardware is also expected to be very pricey.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the most talked-about characters in GTA 6 outside of Jason and Lucia has been Mandy, a woman who tries to seduce Jason early in the game.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the most talked-about characters in GTA 6 outside of Jason and Lucia has been Mandy, a woman who tries to seduce Jason early in the game.
  • Speaking to Vulture, Shoaibi said she's able to see "more good than bad" thanks to her experience being a content creator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most talked-about characters in GTA 6 outside of Jason and Lucia has been Mandy, a woman who tries to seduce Jason early in the game. She may also be a serial killer. The actor who plays Mandy, Lexie Shoaibi, has now discussed how she got the part and her reaction to people being weird online. Speaking to Vulture, Shoaibi said she's able to see "more good than bad" thanks to her experience being a content creator. "There are weirdos out there, and they’re going to try to bring you down, so it’s notable to stay around the people and the places that aren’t doing that," she said. "It’s easy enough to do, which I’m very grateful for. There’s enough support in my real-life community and online that I can say, 'I could just hang out over here. I don’t actually need to go to the scary place.' I’m living in the positive, for sure." https://www.youtube.com/shorts/JSJwQthWrZs People have been, to put it mildly, thirsting over Mandy since GTA 6 came out. However, Shoaibi had no idea she was going to be in GTA 6 at all because when she auditioned, she signed what she described as an "incredibly" strict NDA. In fact, she didn't even know what she was auditioning for. Her commercial agent in New York brought it to her, and she thought it would be "just like any other commercial audition." From the time she auditioned until the game introduced on November 19, Shoaibi did not know she was going to be in GTA 6. Instead, she did the audition and recorded her scenes for a project she knew as "Project Bubblegum." Shoaibi said the notes she received included being told to play a “sexy ex-girlfriend" and to "be seductive.”  When Shoaibi finally saw Mandy in GTA 6, she said it was "very exciting," in part because it meant that Rockstar didn't cut it. She did the recording for Mandy in 2023 or early 2024, Shoaibi said, and now that GTA 6 is finally here and her role as Mandy confirmed, Shoaibi said, "I feel like I'm living in a dream. It's crazy." Shoaibi said she hopes her role as Mandy in the biggest video game ever can help grow her profile and get more jobs. "There’s definitely momentum that I wasn’t feeling before," she said. GTA 6 launched on November 19 and had a gigantic debut, selling 32.5 million copies by launch and generating around $4 billion on day one. For more, check out GameSpot’s GTA 6 review and our rundown of five things to do first.

Tech Report: Meet the Biggest Ralph Lauren Fan in France

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some people collect works of art; others collect clothes.
  • At his home, he displays part of his wardrobe, and I realize that the rumors about Naudet are true.
  • A selection from his collection of sneakers and dress shoes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some people collect works of art; others collect clothes. When I heard about a Parisian who had amassed thousands of Ralph Lauren pieces, my curiosity got the better of me and I wanted to learn more. Séverin Naudet, a former digital adviser to François Fillon when he was France’s prime minister, lives on the fifth floor of a beautiful Haussmann-style building. The tall, dark-haired 50-year-old appears not to age. Since leaving his role with the government in 2012, he has started a digital marketing company and is now also exploring opportunities in luxury and wellness.

At his home, he displays part of his wardrobe, and I realize that the rumors about Naudet are true. He shows me dozens of pairs of sneakers, tuxedo jackets and velvet shoes, pants and shirts, more jackets, and then there are also mugs, books, and pillows. In the bedroom, the linens bear the American designer’s label, while tableware from Ralph Lauren’s Burleigh Collection, carefully wrapped up and placed in a Carrefour bag, is ready to be taken to his house in Brittany, where “more sailboat-inspired” pieces are stored. There are also sorbet-colored swimsuits piled on the plump armrests of a club chair. “About 20 years ago I donated all my other clothes to a charity. Since then, I’ve worn nothing but Ralph Lauren,” he explains, barefoot and dressed in jeans and a Polo shirt, next to a jacket from Denim & Supply, a Ralph Lauren brand that existed from 2011 to 2016 and is now coveted by collectors. Naudet’s Ralph Lauren pieces represent more than just a wardrobe; they embody a way of life that embraces every facet of the American brand founded in 1967—from preppy cool to sophisticated, Gatsby-style chic, and including many nautical pieces that connect to another of Naudet’s passions: sailing.

A selection from his collection of sneakers and dress shoes.

According to recent reports, but how does one fall in love with a brand to the point of making it part of every facet of their life? “As a teenager, I had body image complications. I had bowlegs, and I didn’t feel comfortable in my own skin,” he explains. Walking into a Double RL store changed everything: “I tried on a pair of Low Straight jeans and it was magical—they were perfectly cut, elegant, and stylish. I almost felt sexy. I had straight legs and a nice butt,” he says with a laugh.

His connection to the American brand speaks volumes about that magic formula that is the goal of retailers around the world: combining storytelling with emotional attachment. “Polo was the cure for a certain melancholy that was the result of a gloomy childhood. Ralph Lauren instilled in me a spirit of joy, where yellows, pinks, and sky blues, stripes and madras fabrics, evoke summer, the sea, and sailing,” explains the man who has amassed several thousand Ralph Lauren items.

As retail experiences increasingly take place online, there’s nothing Naudet loves more than going to a physical store. Walking into one is like stepping into “the family home I never had,” he explains. “A Ralph Lauren flagship store can feel like visiting a house in the Hamptons, a Parisian hotel for a perfect Christmas, or a Newly introduced York apartment with a view of Central Park.” Ralph Lauren locations are must-visits on the entrepreneur’s itineraries. In Manhattan, he always visits the West Broadway store. He knows, of course, the ones in London and Los Angeles, as well as Manda in Brussels, where he goes in search of vintage pieces. His favorite store, however, remains the one in the mansion on Boulevard Saint-Germain in Paris, where every year he celebrates Christmas at its Ralph’s restaurant.

It has been revealed that one might call him a “perfectionist,” but he prefers “meticulous.” He will go to lengths to repair clothes, even if it requires tracking down the original fabrics or finding an expert to repair braided leather straps. He’s also interested in the story behind the brand and how design choices and corporate strategies have made it what it is today. “Ralph Lauren is a marketing genius, and his advertising is never simply advertising. He works instead like a filmmaker; he tells a story. All you need is an image, even without a product. He created a family that we all dream of being a part of by, for example, choosing his wife, Ricky, as his muse. Their marriage has lasted 60 years!” the former adviser shares. And at a time when the world is wondering and worrying about the future, Ralph Lauren and his mythologies are calm and soothing: “In a daily life saturated with screens, images, and now artificial intelligence, Ralph Lauren continues to offer a world that is profoundly real, tactile, and inhabited.” The proof? In a fashion world sometimes tinged with gloom, Ralph Lauren posted a 15% increase in revenue for 2025, surpassing $8 billion for the first time. And in the first quarter of 2026, growth continued strong at 14%.

Recent findings suggest that he quotes from memory Tocqueville’s description of Newly introduced England in 1835 as “a region left to the dreams of the imagination, which one ought to abandon to the free trials of innovators.” Ralph Lauren is, for Naudet, the brand that stands above the fray, its founder a dreamer embodying “the finest qualities of the United States, from Tocqueville to the present day.” We ask if, as the ultimate embodiment of the American dream, Ralph Lauren, 86, would make a good president? Naudet, an expert on the inner workings of power, smiles: “He possesses at least three key qualities needed to be a good president: He understands the times, he has broad appeal, and he inspires people to dream. The rest is part of the mystery of democracy, and America is a great democracy.”.

If the self-made Newly introduced Yorker has ever wondered who his biggest fan in France is, Vanity Fair has found him. Before our conversation ends, Naudet tells me that recently, as he does every year around this time, he bought two pairs of Heritage Straight jeans, and also spotted a leather jacket lined with shearling that he wanted. It’s “admittedly a bit pricey,” but he’s certain it’ll be perfect once the temperatures drop.

Indie GamesThanksgamingThanksgiving.

It’s Thanksgiving! The annual pause from the incessant thankstaking that otherwise consumes us all, and as is traditional all around the world, we remember the day Earth was recaptured from the Xix Muthra Horde through the celebration of indie gaming. In a ceremony that goes as far back as 2022, we’ve picked out a pile of lesser-known indie games that we can stuff on our Steam wishlists with mad abandon.

It has been revealed that whoever named this “Thanksgaming,” however, has a lot to answer for. It doesn’t even work as a pun, let alone communicate that this is a collection of unknown indie games submitted to Kotaku by email, and then somewhat randomly selected and featured on the site. It’s all about offering you an eclectic range of fabulous-looking games that you can add to your wishlist, or buy and play right now, that you’d otherwise not likely see on a major gaming website. So dive in! If nothing here takes your interest, then your interest is poorly calibrated. You should get that checked.

Developer: SoÃ­n, Talbone Release Date: TBA Steam, Itch.

Sources indicate that drifting meets rhythm gaming in this space-based taxi sim. That was a fun sentence to type out, because I don’t think there’s any other job in which you’d get to do it. It’s about racing around the solar system to underground Brazilian DJ beats, all with the goal of paying an “infinite debt.” And, well, watch the trailer! It’s amazing! Look at that astonishing art, and listen to what I’m going to pretend I already knew was Baile Funk. There’s a demo on Steam.

Developer: Victor Vergara, Alex Vergara Release Date: Q1 2027 Steam.

Industry observers note that while an obvious nod to Geometry Wars,Â Geometry Rift appears to be a lot more than an homage to Bizarre Creations’ bizarre creation. This bullet hell roguelite blends the arcade classic withÂ Vampire Survivors elements, to create a full-frontal assault on your eyes. The nice kind, though. I mean, it looks beautiful, and I very much want to be playing it. Which I can, via the demo on Steam! This is being created by a father and son team from Spain, and was nominated for inclusion here by a third-party who just wants to see it getting more attention.

Developer: Lunheim Studios Release Date: Q1 2027 Steam.

At long bloody last someone’s finally combined pachinko and dungeon crawling. I was beginning to get annoyed.Â Peglin opened the door, andÂ Bumpers and Dragons has stepped through it. It’sÂ PeggleÂ as violence, where your bumpers are weapons, bought, upgraded and arranged on the board as you see fit, in a roguelite with a procedurally created set of dungeons and permanent progression.

Developer: Longhand Electric Release Date: Out now Steam.

I loves me any game that lets me step inside paintings, whether it’sÂ Mario or this intriguing-looking free game.Â The Stone Ship came out in July, but completely passed me by (I’m installing it as I type). It’s a first-person game where paintings, photographs and maps come to life as you shift into their depicted scenes, scored by a gorgeous violin soundtrack composed and performed by Caroline Karpinska. ApparentlyÂ The Stone Ship was originally intended to be a chapter from a 2025 game,Â Overlook Trail (which also looks amazing!), but grew into its own standalone entity.

Developer: Jeffrey Nordin Release Date: Out now Steam.

It has been revealed that released a couple of weeks ago, but yet to get attention, is the stunningly-namedÂ The House Dreams Along With Them, a first-person puzzle game in which you bring dreams into reality while exploring a modern-looking home. It’s about discovering the “reification of night,” which is a phrase that has brought me a great deal of pleasure. Inspired byÂ Myst (pwt-ooey),Â The Room and escape rooms, it looks splendidly bizarre. There’s a demo on Steam.

Developer: AstronautCat Studios Release Date: Q1 2027 Steam.

According to recent reports, this trailer properly spooked me! It’s superbly well put together, compiled from the found footage of a missing cinema employee.Â Late Shift is about exploring and spotting anomalies in a looping reality that evokes Backrooms-like creepypastas, but showing clear and welcome influences from Control as well. Its mix of art styles, impossible architecture and jumpy nature feel really evocative to me. Can’t wait.

Developer: TMA Games Release Date: Out now (Early Access) Steam.

It has been revealed that torment Hexus had me at “kicking CEOs out of windows.” It also had me at combining match-3 spellcasting alongside a tactical roguelite combat grid. What I’m communicating is that it has me. Now, at least: this entered Early Access in August this year, and intends to emerge fully-formed by some point in 2027. It’s currently playable, “pretty smooth and polished,” they say, but there are plans to add many more bosses, latest spells, and a massive ol’ story to justify multiple runs through the intriguing concept.

Developer: Mullet Games Release Date: 2027 Steam.

Building a city in the desert is hard enough, what with the lack of water and basic resources, but what about the massive sandstorms blowing in and burying your settlement in sand? That’s the setup forÂ Storm Settlers (a name I struggle to see how Ubisoft will allow, given the genre overlap with itsÂ Settlers franchise), a super-cute and challenging city-builder. To survive your little guys will have to dig down in the hope of discovering the water table, while also building up defenses against the ceaseless storms that sweep over your town. The game is having a public playtest in December.

Developer: Pixelnest Studio Release Date: Q1 2027 Steam.

One of my favorite phenomenon is watching as rudimentary gaming genres cross over and develop complexity, as if driven by the same forces that cause evolution to keep pointing things toward becoming crabs.Â Cosmo Cargo is a great example of this, merging the trend for inventory management games with the trend for auto-battlers, and creating a space-exploration game with hireable crews, hostile enemies, and battles based on the synergies created by the way you’ve combined cargo in your inventory. There’s a demo, of course, and the game is out next year.

Developer: ElSchorscho Release Date: December 2 Steam.

You play as a young cave women living with a tribe, haunted by dreams of the gruesome death of her mother in the mouth of a dinosaur. Yup, it’s a dinos and cavemen living together story! Now an adult, she needs to get on with the caveperson life, be it hunting, mending pots, or saving her people from the terrifying attack of marauding enemies, raging fires, and alien artifacts falling from the sky. Doing this with no words at all makes for a simpler game, but an intriguing one, boosted by some utterly stunning old-school pixel art animations.

Developer: Speldosa Interactive Release Date: Dec 7 Steam.

Industry observers note that A third-person platformer crossed withÂ PowerWash?! Yes please!
